title: Screening paper 4
intro: This is a speed paper: 54 questions in 15 minutes, about 17 seconds each. Answer the quick ones first and flag anything that needs working; there’s no minus marking, so guess whatever is left before the timer ends.

stimuli.title: Plant visit notice
stimuli.text: Plant visit, Thursday 9 April 2026. The audit team’s bus leaves the office at 7 am. Bring your firm ID card. Phones are not allowed inside the production hall. The hall closes to visitors at 1 pm; anyone who arrives after that will see only the stores.

stimuli.title: Cheques deposited in one week, by branch

questions.stem: Choose the word or words that fill the blank: “The branch head, as well as two of the stores assistants, ___ checking the stock sheets this morning.”

options.text: is
are
were
have been

questions.reason: The subject is ‘the branch head’. A phrase added with ‘as well as’ does not change the verb, so it stays singular: ‘is’. ‘Are’, ‘were’ and ‘have been’ follow the plural ‘assistants’.

questions.stem: Choose the one word for this: “a written record of what was discussed and decided at a meeting”.

options.text: Agenda
Minutes
Circular
Memo

questions.reason: Minutes record what was discussed and decided. The agenda is the list of items to discuss, written before the meeting; a circular and a memo are notes sent round to people.

questions.stem: What does ‘carry out’ mean in this sentence? “The team will carry out a surprise cash count at the branch on Friday.”

options.text: Remove
Postpone
Perform
Plan

questions.reason: To carry out a task is to do it: the team will perform the count on Friday. ‘Remove’ reads the words literally, and planning is a step that comes before carrying it out.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence has an error? “To close the ledger, / the accountant / requested for / two more days.”

options.text: To close the ledger
the accountant
requested for
two more days

questions.reason: The verb ‘request’ takes its object directly: ‘requested two more days’. ‘For’ goes only with the noun, as in ‘a request for two more days’.

questions.stem: A firm’s rule: articles are never allowed to sign off a working paper themselves; going to the Friday training is optional. Which sentence states the rule exactly?

options.text: Articles must not sign off papers and may attend the training.
Articles need not sign off papers and may attend the training.
Articles may not sign off papers and must attend the training.
Articles must not sign off papers and must attend the training.

questions.reason: ‘Must not’ forbids and ‘may’ permits. ‘Need not’ only says a thing is not required, and ‘must attend’ makes the training compulsory, which the rule does not.

questions.stem:
The first sentence is fixed. Choose the best order for the other three.
First: A client asked our team for a list of its overdue customers.
P. The list came to 37 customers, owing ₹21 lakh in all.
Q. We sent it to the client’s finance head with a one-line summary on top.
R. We sorted the ledger by due date and picked every bill more than 90 days old.

options.text: P, R, Q
R, Q, P
Q, R, P
R, P, Q

questions.reason: The list has to be made (R) before ‘the list’ can be counted (P), and ‘it’ in Q is that finished list, so Q comes last.

questions.stem: Choose the correctly written sentence.

options.text: If I was you, I will call the client before Friday.
If I were you, I would call the client before Friday.
If I would be you, I would call the client before Friday.
If I am you, I would call the client before Friday.

questions.reason: Advice about an imagined situation takes the second conditional: ‘If I were …, I would …’. ‘Would’ never goes in the if-clause, and ‘was … will’ and ‘am … would’ mix two patterns.

questions.stem: Which sentence makes it clear that Tara is the one who checked the bank schedule?

options.text: Kavita emailed Tara after she checked the bank schedule.
After she had checked the bank schedule, Kavita emailed Tara.
Kavita emailed Tara once the bank schedule had been checked.
Kavita emailed Tara after Tara had checked the bank schedule.

questions.reason: Naming Tara in the second part removes the doubt. With ‘she’, either of them could have checked it, and ‘had been checked’ hides who did.

questions.stem: Read the notice. Which statement does it support?

options.text: A team member who arrives at 2 pm can still see the stores.
The whole visit will be over by 1 pm.
Phones may be used in the hall if they are on silent.
Only the audit team will travel on the bus that leaves at 7 am.

questions.reason: After 1 pm the hall is closed but the stores can still be seen, so a 2 pm arrival sees the stores. The notice doesn’t say when the visit ends or who else rides the bus, and it bars phones in the hall.

questions.stem: You asked a client’s accountant for the fixed asset register on 2 June and sent a reminder on 5 June. Which line is best for your second reminder?

options.text: So sorry to trouble you again. Please send the register only if you find some time this week.
This is the third time we are asking. Your delay is holding up our whole team.
Just following up on my email of 5 June.
Please share the fixed asset register by Wednesday 10 June for the depreciation work.

questions.reason: It names the document and a fresh date, and says why it matters, without blame. The apology leaves the date to them, ‘the third time’ blames, and ‘just following up’ names neither the register nor a new date.

questions.stem: A client’s sales are ₹3.5 crore this year, the same as last year, but its operating margin has risen from 9% to 13%. By how much has its operating profit risen?

options.text: ₹1.4 lakh
₹14 lakh
₹31.5 lakh
₹45.5 lakh

questions.reason: Sales did not change, so profit rises by the change in margin, 4 percentage points, on ₹350 lakh. ₹1.4 lakh slips a zero; ₹45.5 lakh and ₹31.5 lakh are this year’s and last year’s whole profit.
questions.working: Rise in margin = 13% − 9% = 4% of sales. ₹3.5 crore = ₹350 lakh. 4% × 350 = ₹14 lakh.

questions.stem: At a client’s plant, one machine is serviced every 10 days and another every 12 days. Both were serviced today. After how many days will both next be serviced on the same day?
questions.reason: The next shared day is the least common multiple of 10 and 12. 120 multiplies them (a shared day, but not the first), 22 adds them, and 36 is a multiple of 12 but not of 10.

questions.stem: How many branches deposited more cheques than the average of the five?
questions.reason: South’s 21 pulls the average down to 44, so four branches are above it. ‘2’ counts the branches above the middle value, 49, not above the average.
questions.working: Total = 52 + 21 + 50 + 49 + 48 = 220. Average = 220 ÷ 5 = 44. Above 44: North 52, East 50, West 49, Central 48 = 4 branches.

questions.stem: Tarang Bags Pvt Ltd sells a backpack for ₹500. Each one costs ₹300 in material and labour (its variable cost), and fixed costs are ₹4,80,000 a year. How many backpacks must it sell in a year to break even?
questions.reason: Each backpack leaves ₹200 (price less variable cost) to cover the fixed costs. 960 divides by the price, 1,600 by the variable cost and 600 by the two added together.

questions.stem: A firm gives an employee an advance of ₹54,000 at 9% a year simple interest, to be repaid with interest after 8 months. How much interest is due?
questions.reason: The rate is for a year, so take 8/12 of it. ₹4,860 is a full year’s interest, ₹38,880 treats 8 months as 8 years, and ₹57,240 is the whole amount repaid, not the interest.

questions.stem: In 7 days, Zubin has vouched 35% of a client’s sales invoices. At the same pace, how many more days will the rest take?

options.text: 9 days
13 days
14 days
20 days

questions.reason: 35% in 7 days is 5% a day, and 65% is left. 20 days is the whole job, 14 doubles the 7 days though 65% is a little less than twice 35%, and 9 divides 65 by 7.

questions.stem: A firm’s two offices are 270 km apart on one highway. At the same moment, an audit senior drives from the first office towards the second at 50 km/h, and a manager drives from the second towards the first at 40 km/h. How far from the first office do they meet?

options.text: 120 km
135 km
150 km
180 km

questions.reason: Driving towards each other, they close the gap at 50 + 40 = 90 km/h, so they meet after 3 hours. 120 km is the manager’s drive, measured from the second office, and 135 km is the halfway point.
questions.working: Time to meet = 270 ÷ (50 + 40) = 3 hours. Senior’s distance = 50 × 3 = 150 km from the first office (manager: 40 × 3 = 120 km from the second).

questions.stem: Medha starts a business with ₹1,50,000. After 4 months, Nirav joins her as a partner with ₹2,00,000. They agree to share profit in the ratio of each one’s capital multiplied by the months it was invested. The first year’s profit is ₹1,19,000. What is Nirav’s share?
questions.reason: Nirav’s money was in for 8 months, not 12. ₹68,000 shares by capital alone (3 : 4), ₹59,500 shares equally and ₹47,600 by months alone (12 : 8).

questions.stem: On any day, the chance that a client replies to a reminder is 1/3, and each client replies independently of the others. You send reminders to three clients today. What is the chance that at least one of them replies?
questions.reason: Find the chance that nobody replies and take it from 1. 8/27 is that ‘nobody’ chance, 4/9 is exactly one reply, and 26/27 is ‘not all three reply’.
questions.working: One client not replying = 2/3. None of the three = 2/3 × 2/3 × 2/3 = 8/27. At least one = 1 − 8/27 = 19/27.

questions.stem: Logarithms here are to base 10. If log x = 3 + log 4, what is x?
questions.reason: 3 is log 1,000, and adding logs multiplies the numbers: x = 1,000 × 4. 1,004 adds them, 1,00,00,000 reads log 4 as 4, and 12 multiplies 3 by 4.

questions.stem: What comes next in the series? 3, 20, 6, 17, 12, 14, 24, ?
questions.reason: Two series take turns: the 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th terms double (3, 6, 12, 24) and the 2nd, 4th and 6th fall by 3 (20, 17, 14). The next term is the 8th, so it belongs to the falling series; 48 continues the doubling one.
questions.working: Odd places: 3, 6, 12, 24 (× 2). Even places: 20, 17, 14 (− 3). The 8th term is an even place: 14 − 3 = 11.

questions.stem: Which word is the odd one out?

options.text: Occurrence
Completeness
Materiality
Accuracy

questions.reason: Occurrence, completeness and accuracy are assertions about transactions: claims in the accounts that an auditor tests. Materiality is the size threshold the auditor uses to judge misstatements, not an assertion.

questions.stem: At Vistar Hospitals Pvt Ltd, every vendor bill above ₹2 lakh goes to the CFO for approval, and the rule is always followed. One vendor bill did not go to the CFO. What follows?

options.text: Its amount cannot be told from this.
It is for more than ₹2 lakh.
The rule was broken for this bill.
It is for ₹2 lakh or less.

questions.reason: Above ₹2 lakh always means the CFO sees the bill, so a bill the CFO did not see cannot be above ₹2 lakh. A broken rule is ruled out because the rule is always followed.

questions.stem: At an induction, new articles stand in one row. Rhea is 8th from the left and Devansh is 14th from the left. They swap places, and Rhea is now 11th from the right. How many articles are in the row?
questions.reason: After the swap Rhea stands where Devansh stood, 14th from the left, and she is counted from both ends, so subtract 1. 18 uses her old place, 25 counts her twice and 22 adds the two places from the left.
questions.working: Rhea’s new place = 14th from the left = 11th from the right. Row = 14 + 11 − 1 = 24.

questions.stem: At about 7:30 am on a clear day, your shadow falls straight ahead of you. Which way are you facing?

options.text: North
South
East
West

questions.reason: In the morning the sun is in the east, and a shadow falls away from the sun, to the west. A shadow in front of you means you face west. ‘East’ is the slip: facing the sun puts your shadow behind you.

questions.stem: In a code, X # Y means X is the son of Y, X @ Y means X is the sister of Y, and X & Y means X is the mother of Y. If L # M @ N, what is L to N?

options.text: Son
Brother
Cousin
Nephew

questions.reason: L is the son of M, and M is the sister of N, so L is the son of N’s sister: N’s nephew. ‘Son’ skips the step through M, and the & code is not used at all.

questions.stem: Six colleagues, Charu, Ishaan, Juhi, Mohit, Hitesh and Yamini, each present once, one after another. Mohit presents immediately before Juhi. Juhi does not present second. Hitesh presents at some point after Yamini. Which of these cannot present first?

options.text: Mohit
Charu
Yamini
Ishaan

questions.reason: If Mohit went first, Juhi would be second, which a clue rules out. Each of the others can open, for example Yamini, Charu, Mohit, Juhi, Ishaan, Hitesh, or the same with Charu or Ishaan first.

questions.stem: A manager says: “If we move the team’s weekly review from Thursday to Monday, fewer files will miss their Friday deadlines.” Which fact, if true, most strengthens this?

options.text: Most late files last quarter were held up by Thursday’s review points.
Most of the team would rather meet on Mondays than on Thursdays.
Some files were late because clients sent their data after the cut-off.
The team handled more files this quarter than last quarter.

questions.reason: If late files were held up by Thursday’s review points, a Monday review leaves four days to clear them by Friday, not one. Preferences don’t change deadlines, and late client data is a cause a Monday review can’t fix, so it weakens the claim.

questions.stem:
Is the monthly rent of a godown more than ₹45,000?
I. After a 20% rise next year, the rent will be ₹57,600.
II. Its rent is ₹6,000 more than that of the office next door.
Which statements, if any, are enough to answer the question?

options.text: Statement I alone is enough, but II alone is not
Statement II alone is enough, but I alone is not
Each statement alone is enough
Both statements together are enough, but neither alone is
Even both statements together are not enough

questions.reason: I gives the rent: ₹57,600 is 120% of it, so it is ₹48,000 and the answer is yes. II needs the office’s rent, which you don’t have.
questions.working: From I: rent = 57,600 ÷ 1.2 = ₹48,000, more than ₹45,000. From II: rent = the office’s rent + 6,000, unknown.

questions.stem: This statement is true: “Tomorrow Aarav will attend the stock count, the bank visit, or both.” Aarav does not attend the bank visit. What follows?

options.text: He attends neither.
He attends both.
He attends the stock count.
Nothing can be said about the stock count.

questions.reason: An ‘or’ statement is true when at least one of its parts is true. The bank visit is out, so the stock count must be the true part; ‘neither’ would make the statement false.

questions.stem: Saptak Hotels Pvt Ltd follows the accrual basis, with a 31 March year-end. Its ₹68,000 electricity bill for March 2026 arrives on 6 April and is paid on 15 April. What does the bill do to its 2025–26 accounts?

options.text: Expense of ₹68,000 and an outstanding liability of ₹68,000
Nothing in 2025–26; it is booked when it is paid in 2026–27
Expense of ₹68,000 and a fall in the bank balance of ₹68,000
A prepaid expense (an asset) of ₹68,000

questions.reason: The power was used in March, so the expense belongs to 2025–26 although the bill came and was paid in April; until it is paid it is a liability. Cash moves only in April, in 2026–27.

questions.stem: Sarvam Life Sciences Pvt Ltd, which follows AS, spends ₹18 lakh in 2025–26 on laboratory research into a new compound; no product is in sight yet. How does AS 26 treat the ₹18 lakh?

options.text: As an expense of 2025–26, when incurred
As an intangible asset, amortised over ten years
As capital work-in-progress until results are known
As a deferred cost, written off over five years

questions.reason: AS 26 has research costs expensed when incurred, because research cannot show that it will bring future benefits. Only development costs that meet all of AS 26’s conditions are capitalised.

questions.stem: Ketan Fabricators Ltd follows AS. It buys a machine for ₹7,60,000 and pays ₹80,000 to install it. The machine should last 8 years and then fetch ₹40,000. What is its yearly straight-line depreciation under AS 10?
questions.reason: The depreciable amount is cost (or an amount substituted for cost) less residual value, and installation is part of cost. ₹90,000 leaves installation out, ₹1,05,000 ignores the residual value and ₹1,10,000 adds it.

questions.stem: Lumina Interiors Pvt Ltd made a profit of ₹45 lakh in 2025–26, yet it struggled to pay its suppliers in March. Which statement best shows where its cash went?

options.text: The statement of profit and loss
The trial balance
The directors’ report
The cash flow statement

questions.reason: Profit counts income and expenses when they are earned or incurred, not when cash moves. The cash flow statement (AS 3) shows cash from operating, investing and financing activities, such as money tied up in debtors and stock or spent on assets.

questions.stem: Rangrez Garments trades in shirts. This year it sold shirts for ₹240 lakh, at a gross margin of 20% of the selling price. What did the shirts it sold cost it?

options.text: ₹48 lakh
₹192 lakh
₹200 lakh
₹288 lakh

questions.reason: A 20% margin on the selling price leaves 80% of sales as the cost of the shirts sold. ₹200 lakh treats the 20% as a mark-up on cost, ₹48 lakh is the gross profit itself and ₹288 lakh adds it to sales.
questions.working: Gross profit = 20% × 240 = ₹48 lakh. Cost of the shirts sold = 240 − 48 = ₹192 lakh.

questions.stem: A ₹12 lakh project brings in ₹4 lakh, ₹5 lakh and ₹6 lakh in years 1, 2 and 3, evenly through each year. Which is right about its payback period?

options.text: 2.4 years, using the average yearly inflow
2.5 years; the method ignores the time value of money
2.5 years; the method allows for the time value of money
3 years, as part-years don’t count

questions.reason: After two years ₹9 lakh is back, and the last ₹3 lakh is half of year 3’s ₹6 lakh. Payback counts rupees as they come, so a rupee in year 3 counts the same as one today: it ignores the time value of money.
questions.working: Years 1–2: 4 + 5 = ₹9 lakh. Still to recover: 12 − 9 = ₹3 lakh. 3 ÷ 6 = 0.5 of year 3. Payback = 2.5 years. (12 ÷ the average of 5 = 2.4 years is the slip.)

questions.stem: Akash Tours and Megh Travels each have sales of ₹100 lakh and operating profit of ₹20 lakh. Fixed operating costs are ₹50 lakh at Akash and ₹10 lakh at Megh. Which is right?

options.text: Megh’s operating leverage is higher: its variable costs are higher.
Their operating leverage is equal, as their profits are equal.
It depends on their loans, so it can’t be told.
Akash’s is higher: its profit swings more when sales change.

questions.reason: Operating leverage comes from fixed operating costs. With more of its costs fixed, Akash’s profit moves more for each change in sales. Loans and interest belong to financial leverage.
questions.working: Contribution = operating profit + fixed costs. Degree of operating leverage = contribution ÷ operating profit. Akash: (20 + 50) ÷ 20 = 70 ÷ 20 = 3.5. Megh: (20 + 10) ÷ 20 = 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5.

questions.stem: An article tests 40 of a client’s 2,000 sales invoices and uses the results to conclude on all 2,000. Which standard deals with this?

options.text: SA 505, External Confirmations
SA 530, Audit Sampling
SA 520, Analytical Procedures
SA 580, Written Representations

questions.reason: Testing some items of a population to reach a conclusion on the whole of it is audit sampling, which SA 530 covers. SA 505 is about confirmations from third parties and SA 520 about comparing figures and trends.

questions.stem: The client’s accountant prepares the March bank reconciliation. From the March bank statement and cash book, the auditor prepares the reconciliation again, independently, and compares it with the client’s. Which audit procedure is this?

options.text: Recalculation
Observation
Inquiry
Reperformance

questions.reason: Reperformance is the auditor carrying out again, independently, a procedure or control the client performed. Recalculation only checks the arithmetic of a document, such as re-adding its totals.

questions.stem: An article compares the last 20 sales invoices of March 2026 with the client’s dispatch register and finds three invoices dated 31 March for goods dispatched on 2 April. Which assertion is this test about?

options.text: Cut-off
Occurrence
Completeness
Existence

questions.reason: Cut-off asks whether transactions are recorded in the right period: these three sales belong to April, not March. Occurrence asks whether a sale happened at all, and these did.

questions.stem: Management won’t correct a misstatement in inventory that the auditor judges to be material but not pervasive. Under SA 705, which opinion does the auditor give?

options.text: An unmodified opinion with an Emphasis of Matter paragraph
An adverse opinion
A qualified opinion
A disclaimer of opinion

questions.reason: A material misstatement that is not pervasive leads to a qualified, ‘except for’, opinion. Adverse is for misstatements that are material and pervasive, a disclaimer for evidence that can’t be obtained where the possible effect is pervasive, and an Emphasis of Matter never replaces a modified opinion.

questions.stem: Kanak Exports Pvt Ltd, registered under GST with a ₹40 crore turnover, pays an advocate for legal services, which are notified for reverse charge when supplied to a business entity. Who pays the GST on the fee?

options.text: The advocate, on the bill as usual
The company, but only if the advocate is unregistered
The company, as the recipient of the service
No one: reverse charge means no tax is due

questions.reason: Under reverse charge the recipient, not the supplier, pays the tax on notified services such as an advocate’s legal services to a business entity, whether or not the advocate is registered. The company pays it in cash, then claims credit under the normal conditions.

questions.stem: Rekha has held a residential plot as an investment since 2019. In tax year 2026–27, which of these gives rise to capital gains for her?

options.text: Its market value rises by ₹8 lakh during the year
She sells it for more than she paid for it
She gets an offer above her cost but does not sell
She buys a second plot next to it

questions.reason: Capital gains arise only on the transfer of a capital asset, such as a sale. A rise in value or an offer she turns down transfers nothing, and buying a plot gives her an asset, not a gain.

questions.stem: Siya holds 2,000 shares of ₹10 each, ₹6 a share paid, in Ananta Textiles Ltd, a company limited by shares. It is wound up owing more than it owns. What is the most Siya can be asked to pay?

options.text: Her share of all the company’s debts

questions.reason: In a company limited by shares, a member’s liability is limited to the amount unpaid on the shares: ₹4 a share. ₹12,000 is what she has already paid, and ₹20,000 is the full face value.

questions.stem: In 2026–27, the accountant of Ankur Foods Pvt Ltd edits a posted sales entry in its accounting software. Under the Companies (Accounts) Rules, what must the software do?

options.text: Keep only the latest version, once a director approves
Log the edit and its date in an audit trail that can’t be switched off
Print each edit every month for the Registrar
Keep the audit trail running unless the Board resolves to switch it off

questions.reason: From the financial year starting 1 April 2023, a company keeping its books in software must use software that records an audit trail of every transaction, with an edit log of each change and its date, and the trail cannot be disabled. The auditor reports on it.

questions.stem: You’re building an input tax credit summary from a 2,400-row purchase register; 96 rows have no supplier GSTIN. What do you do first?

options.text: Drop them; credit needs a GSTIN anyway
Fill each blank from that supplier’s other invoices
Carry on; 96 rows are only 4%
Check what those rows are, and ask the client why

questions.reason: A blank GSTIN can mean an unregistered supplier, an import or a data fault, and each changes the credit. Dropping, filling in or ignoring the rows guesses at the answer; find out first.

questions.stem: After your senior reviews your debtors’ working paper, a customer’s letter arrives disputing a ₹6 lakh balance you concluded was recoverable. What do you do?

options.text: File the letter, as the paper is already reviewed
Overwrite the old conclusion, so the file reads cleanly
Tell your senior, assess the letter and update the paper
Mark the ₹6 lakh as irrecoverable in your paper straight away

questions.reason: New evidence about a balance you concluded on must be assessed and shown in the file, and your senior must know that reviewed work is changing. Overwriting hides the change, filing the letter ignores it, and marking the balance irrecoverable at once concludes before you have assessed it.

questions.stem: The audit is over budget. Your senior suggests testing 15 payment vouchers, not the planned 40, though the assessed risk is unchanged. What do you do?

options.text: Test the 15 your senior suggests, and note the budget cut in the file
Test all 40 after hours, without recording the time
Ask the client to confirm the other 25 in writing
Tell your senior the risk is unchanged, and agree a sample to match

questions.reason: The sample follows the risk, not the budget. Noting the cut doesn’t make the evidence enough, unrecorded hours hide what the work really took, and the client’s written word is no substitute for testing the vouchers.

questions.stem: An uncle who trades shares asks if a listed client you audit will report good results. You’ve seen the draft numbers. What do you do?

options.text: Say only that they look ‘fine’, without any figures
Suggest waiting for the announcement before buying
Say you can’t discuss clients, and give no hint either way
Share the figures; family members aren’t covered by the rules

questions.reason: Unpublished results are price-sensitive: the audit team gets them for the audit and must keep them confidential. ‘Fine’ and ‘wait’ are hints too, and anyone who trades on them is trading on inside information.

questions.stem: A teammate locked out of the firm’s audit software asks to use your login tonight to finish their notes. What do you do?

options.text: Share it, then change your password tomorrow
Share it only if your senior agrees
Log in yourself, then let them finish their notes on your laptop
Say no, and suggest they ask IT to unlock their account

questions.reason: A login records who did each piece of work, so anything done under yours is recorded as yours. A later password change, a senior’s nod or logging in for them doesn’t change that; IT can unlock their account.

questions.stem: While vouching purchases, you see a vendor whose address is the purchase manager’s home address in the payroll; that manager approved all its bills. What do you do first?

options.text: Ask the purchase manager to explain the link
Note the facts and tell your senior, not the client’s staff
Quietly ask the client’s accountant if anyone has noticed
Leave it, since every bill was approved and the goods arrived

questions.reason: A possible fraud goes to your senior first, with the facts you saw, so the engagement team decides the next step. Raising it with the manager or other staff can warn the people involved; leaving it ignores a red flag.

questions.stem: You tested 25 of a client’s 3,000 sales invoices and found no errors. Which conclusion does your work support?

options.text: No errors in the 25 tested; nothing suggests sales are misstated
All sales for the year are correctly recorded
Sales could not be verified this year
Sales are correctly recorded, as the client’s billing system is reliable

questions.reason: A sample lets you conclude that nothing suggests a misstatement (A), not that every sale is right (B). The system’s reliability wasn’t tested, and ‘could not be verified’ undersells work that was done.

questions.stem: Your senior asks you to tick 300 vouchers against the cash book. It feels like clerical work. What do you do?

options.text: Tick a sample; nobody checks every tick
Get the client’s junior to tick them
Do it carefully, note anything odd, then ask what to take up next
Tell your senior you’d rather do analysis work, as ticking teaches little

questions.reason: Ticking is where you learn how the client’s money moves, and odd items often turn up there. Skipping ticks leaves work undone, handing it to client staff has the client check its own records, and asking for other work before finishing reads badly.

questions.stem: Many companies must file their financial statements with the Ministry of Corporate Affairs in XBRL. What does filing in XBRL do?

options.text: Puts each figure in a form that software can read and compare
Converts the statements from AS to Ind AS
Has the Registrar audit the statements before they can be filed
Locks the statements so that only the company can open them

questions.reason: XBRL (Extensible Business Reporting Language) tags each figure so that computers can read, check and compare filings. It changes the format, not the accounting standards, and it is not an audit.
